stem: How did the telephone most change the way large American businesses operated?

Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alexander_Graham_Bell%27s_Telephone_Patent_Drawing_and_Oath_-_NARA_-_302052_%28page_2%29.jpg
stimulus.text: The image is a page from Alexander Graham Bell's patent application. At the top it reads "A. G. BELL. TELEGRAPHY. No. 174,465. Patented March 7, 1876." Below are two labeled diagrams: Fig. 6 shows three panels of electrical instruments wired together, and Fig. 7 shows a transmitter and receiver joined by a wire. At the bottom, the inventor signs "A. Graham Bell."

options.text: Managers in far-apart cities could talk at once, instead of waiting for letters
Businesses no longer needed railroads, since orders could travel by phone
options.misconception: Background: orders still had to travel as goods on trains; the phone carried words, not freight.

options.text: Small shops replaced big corporations, since anyone could now call a customer
options.misconception: Background: the telephone helped big firms coordinate across distance; it did not break them into small shops.

options.text: Written contracts disappeared, since a phone call counted as a legal agreement
options.misconception: Background: businesses still used written contracts; a phone call could arrange a deal, but it did not replace the paperwork.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the telephone let corporations with a national reach coordinate quickly, because a manager in one city could speak to a manager in another at once. Letters took days and telegrams took hours.
rationales.B: Background: goods still moved by rail, and the railroads kept growing after the telephone arrived. The phone moved words, not wheat or steel.
rationales.C: Background: the telephone favored firms big enough to run offices in many cities. It helped corporations grow, not shrink into small shops.
rationales.D: Background: businesses kept written contracts and records. A phone call arranged business faster, but the paperwork stayed.
rationales.general:
Think about what a manager waits for: an answer.
1. Background: before the telephone, orders and questions crossed the country by letter or by telegram, slowly and in writing.
2. Background: the telephone let a manager in Chicago speak to a manager in New York at once, so a national firm could act as one firm.
3. Background: that speed is why the telephone became a business tool first and a household tool second.
Remember: a tool that kills waiting time changes who can run a big business.
